why: Sodium is so reactive it kicks hydrogen out of water, releasing gas and heat fast enough to spark.
Potassium is even more reactive than sodium, so it reacts with water violently, often catching fire.
Calcium reacts steadily with water, releasing hydrogen bubbles and gentle heat.
Lithium reacts with water but more gently than sodium or potassium, fizzing quietly.
Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but faster with steam, releasing hydrogen.
Magnesium combines with oxygen in a bright white flame to form magnesium oxide.
Calcium combines directly with oxygen to form quicklime, releasing heat.
Iron slowly combines with oxygen in moist air, forming the reddish-brown compound we call rust.
Copper reacts with oxygen when heated, forming a black surface coating.
Zinc burns in oxygen to form a white powder, zinc oxide.
Potassium is reactive enough to grab extra oxygen atoms, forming a superoxide.
Aluminum reacts with oxygen to form a tough oxide layer, which is why it resists corrosion.
Sodium reacts with oxygen readily, forming a pale yellow peroxide compound.
Lithium combines with oxygen to form a simple white oxide.
Lead reacts slowly with oxygen at its surface, forming a dull oxide coating.
Tin combines with oxygen when heated, forming a stable oxide.
Nickel reacts with oxygen at high temperature, forming a green-black oxide.
Manganese combines with oxygen when heated, forming a mixed oxide.
Nitrogen is normally unreactive, so it only combines with oxygen when given a lot of energy, like lightning.
Carbon burns in oxygen, releasing energy as heat and light, the same reaction that powers a charcoal fire.
Sulfur burns with a blue flame in oxygen, releasing a sharp-smelling gas.
Hydrogen burns explosively in oxygen, releasing a huge burst of energy and forming water.
Sodium displaces hydrogen from the acid, forming common table salt and hydrogen gas.
Magnesium reacts with the acid, pushing out hydrogen gas as bubbles.
Calcium reacts with the acid, releasing hydrogen and forming a soluble salt.
Iron slowly dissolves in the acid, releasing hydrogen bubbles.
Zinc reacts readily with the acid, a classic lab demonstration of hydrogen gas production.
Aluminum reacts with the acid once its protective oxide layer is broken, releasing hydrogen.
Lithium reacts with the acid, forming a soluble chloride salt and hydrogen gas.
Tin reacts slowly with the acid, releasing hydrogen over time.
Nickel reacts slowly with the acid, forming a green-tinted salt solution.
Manganese reacts readily with the acid, releasing hydrogen gas.
Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it can't displace hydrogen from the acid.
Silver is far below hydrogen in reactivity, so it stays completely unaffected by the acid.
Lead forms an insoluble chloride coating on its surface that blocks further reaction.
Zinc is amphoteric, meaning it can react with both acids and bases, releasing hydrogen either way.
Aluminum is also amphoteric and reacts with strong bases, releasing hydrogen gas.
This is a classic neutralization: the acid and base cancel each other out, leaving table salt and water.
Chlorine gas combines with slaked lime to form bleaching powder, used for disinfecting water.
When carbon dioxide is bubbled through sodium hydroxide solution, it forms baking soda.
Heating baking soda breaks it down into washing soda's core compound, releasing carbon dioxide and water vapor.
Heating gypsum drives off most of its water, leaving the semi-hydrated powder known as plaster of Paris.
